mints.name: Roma (Rome): Moneta
mints.locNote: Republican mint traditionally by the temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx [12.4829, 41.8937]; the imperial mint lay in Regio III near San Clemente, where dedications by the officinatores of Trajan's mint (CIL VI 42-44) were found.
marks: (none: moneyer names and control marks, Republic)
officina numerals P S T Q V VI ... XII in field (3rd c.)
mints.officinae: Republic: unknown number of workshops under the tresviri monetales. Up to 12 officinae under Gallienus; 6-7 after 274; usually 4 (P, S, T, Q) in the 4th c., sometimes more; one or two in the Byzantine period.
mints.notes: The longest-lived mint of antiquity, striking from the aes grave of the early 3rd c. BC to the papal and Byzantine coinage of the 7th-8th centuries. Republican coins carry no mint mark: they are signed by the moneyers (IIIviri aere argento auro flando feriundo) and from c. 140 BC increasingly advertise their families, which is why the Republican series is studied by moneyer and dated by Crawford's die-link and hoard sequence (RRC). Many late Republican issues carry control marks (letters, numerals, symbols) marking individual dies: Piso Frugi (RRC 340) and the moneyers of the 80s used hundreds. Under Augustus gold and silver moved to Lugdunum c. 15-12 BC, while Rome struck the moneyers' aes (signed IIIVIR AAAFF until c. 4 BC); Nero restored precious-metal production at Rome by 64. In 271 the mint workers under the rationalis Felicissimus rebelled against Aurelian and were crushed with heavy loss (Aurelius Victor gives 7,000 soldiers killed); the mint was cut down and reorganised. From 294 Rome uses R plus officina letter; Maxentius (306-312) made it a showcase (Romulus and Remus, temple of Roma AETERNAE). In the 4th c. look for RP, RS, RT, RQ, often with a wreath or star; from the 370s SMROM and RMPS (silver). Late gold reads COMOB with R M flanking. Under Odoacer and the Ostrogoths Rome struck large bronze (40 nummi with INVICTA ROMA, she-wolf, eagle) that copied the old sestertius look; after 552 Byzantine Rome struck gold of a recognisable fine, small-flan style, silver fractions and decanummia with ROMA or ROM.

mints.name: Romano-Campanian mint(s), probably Neapolis
mints.notes: Rome's first silver was struck in Campania on the Greek didrachm (c. 7.3 g, falling to c. 6.7 g) for a state that did not yet strike silver at home. The earliest piece, the Mars/horse head didrachm reading ROMANO (RRC 13), is usually dated c. 310-300 and attributed to Neapolis, whose die-cutters' style it shares; Crawford placed it c. 280-275, connecting it with the Pyrrhic War and the Via Appia. The series continues with Apollo/horse (ROMANO), Hercules/she-wolf and twins (ROMANO, RRC 20, c. 269-266), Mars/horse head (ROMA), Roma/Victory, and ends with the quadrigatus (Janus/Jupiter in quadriga with Victory, ROMA incuse on a tablet, RRC 28-34) struck in very large numbers c. 225-212 to pay for the Gallic and Hannibalic wars and debased during the crisis. Associated bronze and the Janus/oath-scene gold staters and half-staters (RRC 28-29, c. 216) belong to the same system. Identification: the earliest pieces read ROMANO, later ROMA; all are didrachms or fractions on the Campanian standard, never denarii; the quadrigatus can be hard to tell from imitations struck by allies. Mint location is still argued: Neapolis, Capua, Rome itself, or several mints.

mints.name: Luceria (Lucera), auxiliary mint of the Second Punic War
mints.notes: One of several mints that Rome operated outside the city during the Hannibalic war. Coins with the monogram or letter L (Crawford RRC 97-99) are assigned to the Latin colony of Luceria in Apulia, close to the main Roman armies facing Hannibal. Output includes early denarii, quinarii and sestertii, victoriati and bronze on the reduced sextantal standard. Pieces of the 'L' series are among those that tie the denarius to c. 211: their associated bronze sits at the sextantal stage. Similar regional series carry other symbols (a corn-ear for Sicily, KA, CA, MA and monograms whose attribution remains open).

mints.name: Sicilian mint of the corn-ear series
mints.notes: Coins with a corn-ear (Crawford's 'corn-ear' group, including the gold 60/40/20 as pieces marked with value numerals and early denarii and victoriati) are attributed to a Roman mint operating in Sicily during and after the siege of Syracuse (213-211). The corn-ear points to Sicilian grain. The group matters for dating: excavations at Morgantina, sacked by the Romans in 211, found early denarii and associated issues sealed in the destruction levels, the strongest archaeological evidence for Crawford's c. 211 date for the introduction of the denarius against the older 187 or 269 dates.

mints.name: Corfinium renamed Italia (Social War rebel mint)
mints.notes: The confederated Italians made Corfinium their capital, renamed it Italia, and struck denarii on the Roman standard, consciously answering Roman types. Obverses show the head of Italia (laureate or helmeted); reverses include an oath scene with warriors touching a sow with their swords, the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf, Dioscuri and a warrior with a bull. Legends are Latin (ITALIA) or Oscan (VITELIU, the name of the commanders Q. Poppaedius Silo and C. Papius Mutilus in Oscan script). As the war turned, production shifted to Bovianum and Aesernia. Many issues are overstruck on Roman denarii, which shows where the silver came from. All are rare and heavily faked; genuine pieces have the flat, shallow relief and slightly irregular flans of the Roman denarius of the 90s, and die studies (Campana) list most known dies.

mints.name: Paestum (last civic mint of Italy)
mints.notes: The Latin colony of 273 BC kept the right to strike small bronze long after every other Italian community had stopped. Its semisses and quadrantes of the late Republic and early Principate carry PS S C (Paestum, by decree of the local senate) and the names of local magistrates; a few issues name Tiberius, and the series ends under him. Collectors meet them as small, crude, heavily patinated bronzes with Bona Mens, a cornucopia or a temple. They are the last flicker of the civic coinages of Italy, which the Roman state otherwise absorbed by the end of the Social War.

mints.name: Bolskan / Osca (Huesca): Iberian denarius mint
mints.notes: The most prolific of the Iberian denarius mints of the Ebro valley. Bolskan denarii (bearded male head right / horseman with lance) were struck on the Roman weight standard from the mid-2nd century, apparently to pay native levies and taxes in Roman service, and production peaked in the 80s-70s when Osca was Sertorius' capital (Plutarch, Sertorius 14, his school for noble Iberian boys). Their mass in Spanish hoards that close in the 70s is a principal witness to the cost of the Sertorian war. Many other Iberian mints (Turiasu, Sekobirikes, Arekorata, Ikalesken) struck the same types; identification depends on reading the Iberian legend under the horseman. Common, but beware cast copies.

mints.name: Massalia (Marseille)
mints.notes: Rome's oldest overseas friend struck silver from the late 6th century: drachms (Artemis / lion) on a light standard close to the Roman victoriatus, abundant obols (Apollo / wheel with MA), and bronze (Apollo / bull). Massaliot drachms were widely imitated in the Po valley and the Alps, where 'Padane drachms' with corrupt lion types formed a separate currency. Caesar's siege of 49 BC and the city's capitulation ended its political independence and, on the usual view, its silver coinage. Identification: obols are tiny (c. 0.6-0.7 g) with a four-spoked wheel; the Celtic imitations have stylised, often unreadable legends.

mints.name: Utica: Pompeian military mint in Africa
mints.notes: After Pharsalus the Pompeian leadership regrouped in Africa and struck denarii and some gold at a mint usually placed at Utica, where Cato commanded. Types: Metellus Scipio's elephant (an allusion to his family's victory at Panormus in 250 BC) and the African genius with lion skin; Cato's Roma seated / VICTRIX; Eppius' Hercules. Juba I of Numidia struck his own denarii (bearded king / temple, REX IVBA in Latin and Neo-Punic) at an uncertain royal mint, on the same standard, showing how closely the war finance was shared. The Thapsus campaign (46) ended the series. Rare to scarce; Scipio's elephant denarius is the common one.

mints.name: Emerita Augusta (Mérida)
mints.notes: Founded in 25 BC by Augustus' legate P. Carisius for veterans of the Cantabrian war (V Alaudae and X Gemina). Carisius struck denarii, quinarii and some aurei: the bare head of Augustus with IMP CAESAR AVGVST and reverses of captured Cantabrian weapons (helmet, double axe, sword, round shield), a trophy and the city gate with EMERITA over the arch, one of the earliest city views on Roman coins. Thereafter the colony struck bronze under Augustus, Tiberius and Caligula (priest ploughing the pomerium, city gate, Divus Augustus with altar). Carisius' denarii are scarce and prized for the gate type; check the gate's two arches and the inscription spacing against published dies.

mints.name: Colonia Patricia (Córdoba), Augustan 'Spanish' mint
mints.notes: RIC I² assigns a large Augustan gold and silver coinage of c. 19-16 BC, struck in the aftermath of the Cantabrian wars and the Parthian settlement, to Colonia Patricia, with other groups to an uncertain second Spanish mint (often thought to be Caesaraugusta or Emerita). Types: the oak-wreathed head of Augustus (CAESAR AVGVSTVS), SIGNIS RECEPTIS with standards and the clipeus virtutis (CL V), the Parthian kneeling with a standard, the round temple of Mars Ultor holding the recovered standards, the comet of Divus Iulius, OB CIVIS SERVATOS. Without mint marks, attribution rests on style (fuller portraits than Rome's) and hoard distribution, and the location has been argued for a century. These are the commonest Augustan denarii after the Gaius-Lucius type of Lugdunum.

mints.name: Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza), colonial mint
mints.notes: Veteran colony of veterans from IV Macedonica, VI Victrix and X Gemina, whose numbers appear on its bronzes with vexilla and aquila. The founding type shows the priest ploughing the sacred furrow with a yoke of oxen. Names of local duoviri date issues; series run from Augustus to Caligula, when Spanish civic coinage ends (traditionally linked to Caligula's displeasure, though the mechanism is unknown). Large, well-made asses and dupondii of Tiberius (with Augustus as DIVVS) and Caligula's issues for Agrippina and Germanicus are popular with collectors.

mints.name: Tarraco (Tarragona)
mints.notes: The colony (Colonia Victrix Togata Tarraco or Iulia Urbs Triumphalis) struck bronze under Augustus and Tiberius, notably the altar with a palm sprouting from it, the omen reported to Augustus and answered with his famous joke that this showed how often they sacrificed (Quintilian 6.3.77). In 68 Galba, proclaimed in Spain, struck aurei and denarii there and at other Spanish mints (HISPANIA, SALVS GEN HVMANI, Roma and Victory types, and the 'autonomous' civil-war denarii without portraits). Vespasian's earliest western gold and silver (69-70) is also attributed to Tarraco by RIC II²; it is usually recognised by a tiny globe at the point of the bust and by distinctive lettering.

mints.name: Colonia Nemausus (Nîmes)
mints.notes: Struck the most recognisable colonial bronze of the West: back-to-back heads of Agrippa (with rostral crown) and Augustus, IMP DIVI F, and reverse a crocodile chained to a palm tree with COL NEM, celebrating the conquest of Egypt and the settlement of veterans of the Egyptian campaign. Three main series (c. 28 BC, c. 16-10 BC, c. AD 10-14) can be separated by Augustus' laurel wreath and the P P (pater patriae, after 2 BC) on the last. Specimens are very often cut in half, because they circulated as small change across Gaul and on the Rhine; a rare variant has a leg-shaped flange ('pied de sanglier'), probably a votive form. Large numbers turn up in German military sites before AD 9.

mints.name: Lugdunum (Lyon)
marks: (none, 15 BC-AD 69; globe at bust point on Nero's aes)
mints.officinae: 3 under the Tetrarchy and Constantine (P, S, T); 2 in the later 4th c.
mints.notes: Augustus made the capital of the Three Gauls his main gold and silver mint around 15 BC (Strabo 4.3.2 notes gold and silver struck there). It produced the Gaius and Lucius Caesares denarius (2 BC-AD 4, the commonest Augustan denarius) and Tiberius' 'tribute penny' (PONTIF MAXIM, seated female often identified as Livia), plus the great 'Altar of Lugdunum' series of asses, semisses and sesterces with the Altar of Rome and Augustus (ROM ET AVG), dedicated 12/10 BC. Precious-metal production returned to Rome under Caligula. Nero reopened it for aes in 64-67: Lugdunum Neronian sestertii and asses are identified by a small globe at the point of the bust. Galba, Vitellius and Vespasian struck aes here; Clodius Albinus struck his own denarii and aurei in 195-197. Aurelian reopened the mint in 274 with personnel from the closed Gallic mint at Cologne. In the 4th c. look for PLG/SLG, later LVGD, LVGP, LVGS, with crescents, stars and pellets; gold with LVGOB is rare. It ended with the usurpers of 407-413.

mints.name: Colonia Agrippina (Cologne), Gallic Empire mint
mints.notes: The usurpation of Postumus in 260 created a separate western coinage that lasted until Tetricus' surrender in 274. Two mints are distinguished by style and hoard evidence ('Mint I' and 'Mint II'): older literature put them at Lyon and Cologne, more recent work at Trier and Cologne, and the identifications are still argued. Postumus' early antoniniani were noticeably better than Gallienus' (c. 15-20% silver) and his gold is among the finest of the century, with superb facing portraits and Hercules labours. The fineness collapsed under Victorinus and the Tetrici to a few per cent. Cologne's coins are recognised by a distinctive Postumus portrait and by reverse groups such as SAECVLI FELICITAS; Laelianus and Marius are associated with Mainz/Cologne style. When Aurelian reunified the empire the staff went to Lugdunum.

mints.name: Treveri (Trier)
mints.officinae: 2 (P, S) normally; A and B under the Tetrarchy.
mints.notes: Probably already a Gallic Empire mint, Trier became a regular imperial mint when Constantius I made it his capital in 293/4. It was the main western gold mint of the 4th century: the Beaurains (Arras) treasure contains Trier solidi and multiples, and Trier struck enormous numbers of nummi for Constantine's GLORIA EXERCITVS, VRBS ROMA and CONSTANTINOPOLIS types (330-335) and for Constantine II. Marks: PTR/STR (officina first) and TRP/TRS (officina last), with crescents, dots and wreaths that identify sub-issues; precious-metal marks TROB (gold, OB = obryzum, refined) and TRPS (silver, PS = pusulatum) from c. 367. Magnentius and Decentius struck here in quantity (big CHI-RHO 'Salus' bronzes, 353), as did Magnus Maximus and Flavius Victor (383-388). After the praetorian prefecture moved to Arles c. 395-407, Trier struck only for Constantine III (407-411) and Jovinus (411-413).

mints.name: Londinium (London), later Augusta
mints.notes: Opened by Carausius (286/7-293) and continued by Allectus (293-296), who marked coins L or ML (moneta Londiniensis) and, after an attempt to align with the central coinage, ML XXI. The enigmatic silver denarii and gold of Carausius with RSR in the exergue (expanded as Redeunt Saturnia Regna, from Virgil Eclogue 4.6, a reading backed by the INPCDA medallion) belong to the start of the revolt; their mint is uncertain. After Constantius I recovered Britain in 296 London struck unmarked folles, then LON, and under Constantine PLN, PLON, MLL and MLN (marks on which numismatists still argue), with the SOLI INVICTO COMITI, BEATA TRANQVILLITAS (VOTIS XX altar) and VIRTVS EXERCIT types. Closed c. 325. Magnus Maximus revived it under the city's new name Augusta: AVGOB solidi and AVGPS siliquae of Maximus are great rarities, almost the only 'London' coins after 325. Identification: Carausian radiates with S P or S C in the field and ML/L in the exergue; 'C' marks belong to the second Carausian mint.

mints.name: 'C' mint of Carausius and Allectus (Camulodunum?)
mints.notes: The second British mint of the usurpers, marked C. Camulodunum (Colchester) is the traditional identification; Clausentum (Bitterne), Glevum (Gloucester) and a mint travelling with the court have also been proposed, and QC has even been read Quinarius Camuloduni or Clausentensis. C-mint radiates tend to be cruder than London's and carry more unusual reverse types (PAX with vertical sceptre is common to both). Allectus' C-mint quinarii with a galley (VIRTVS AVG, QC) are a characteristic denomination: a small radiate weighing about half the normal coin, whose real function is debated.

mints.name: Ambianum (Amiens)
mints.notes: Opened by Magnentius, who was born at Amiens according to tradition, during his usurpation. It struck the standard Magnentian bronze types (VICTORIAE DD NN AVG ET CAES, two Victories holding a wreath inscribed VOT V MVLT X, and the great chi-rho with alpha and omega, SALVS DD NN AVG ET CAES) for Magnentius and his Caesar Decentius, plus rare gold. It closed after Constantius II's victory. The short life and single dynasty make Amiens pieces scarce and sought after; the AMB mark is unambiguous.

mints.name: Arelate (Arles), renamed Constantina
mints.notes: Constantine transferred the staff of Maxentius' Ostia mint to Arles in 313. Early marks are ARL with officina letters, often with wreaths, stars and crescent; in 328 the city was renamed Constantina (perhaps in honour of Constantine II, whose seat it was) and the mark becomes CONST (Constantina), later KONSTAN and, under Constans and Constantius, PCON, SCON, TCON. The key identification trap: these CON marks with a Latin officina letter in front belong to Arles, whereas Constantinople writes CONS followed by a Greek officina letter. From the 360s Arles returns to marks such as SCON, TCON, then SMARL. Arles was a major gold mint for the western court in the 5th c. (prefecture of the Gauls moved there c. 407): Constantine III, Jovinus, Valentinian III, Avitus (proclaimed at Arles 455), Majorian and Libius Severus struck solidi and tremisses with AR or A-R flanking the figure, before the Visigothic takeover in 476.

mints.name: Mediolanum (Milan)
mints.notes: Gallienus founded the mint c. 259/260 to pay the new cavalry army based at Milan; antoniniani carry P, S, T or MP, MS, MT and the 'legionary' series honouring individual legions with their badges (LEG II ADIVTRIX VI P VI F) belongs here (a rich collecting series). In 268 Aureolus, besieged at Milan, struck coins in Postumus' name with CONCORD EQVIT and other cavalry-themed reverses. Aurelian moved the mint to Ticinum in 274. Milan reopened for precious metals in the later 4th c. as an imperial residence: MDOB solidi, MDPS siliquae of Valentinian I, Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, Magnus Maximus and Eugenius. Honorius' move to Ravenna (402) reduced it; solidi with M-D in the field continue for 5th-century western emperors (Valentinian III, Majorian, Anthemius) and for Odoacer in Zeno's name.

mints.name: Ticinum (Pavia)
mints.officinae: 3-6; four (P, S, T, Q) normally under the Tetrarchy.
mints.notes: Aurelian transferred the Milan mint here in 274. It struck heavily for Aurelian, Probus (huge variety of bust types, a favourite of specialists: helmeted, cuirassed, with shield and spear, with eagle-tipped sceptre), Carus and family, Diocletian and Maximian, then the Tetrarchic folles (GENIO POPVLI ROMANI) and the coinages of Maxentius and Constantine. Ticinum produced several famous gold multiples and the 315 silver medallion of Constantine with the chi-rho on his helmet (the 'Ticinum medallion'), a key document for his Christian symbolism. Closed in 326, its staff probably moving to Constantinople. A later Ostrogothic and Lombard mint at Pavia belongs to another period.

mints.name: Aquileia
mints.notes: Opened in Diocletian's reform of 294. Aquileia's Tetrarchic folles and Constantinian nummi are common; it struck notable gold for Constantine and Licinius and, in the later 4th century, AQOB solidi and AQPS siliquae for Valentinian I, Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, Magnus Maximus (who held it 387-388) and Eugenius. Theodosius defeated Maximus near Aquileia (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus nearby (394), and coin output tracks these campaigns. Activity dwindled in the early 5th century; issues for Joannes (423-425) and the Theodosian house are the last. Identification: AQ marks with dots and palm-branch symbols separate many short emissions in the 330s-350s.

mints.name: Ravenna
mints.notes: The mint followed Honorius' court to Ravenna in 402 and became the main western gold mint, striking solidi with R-V in the field for Honorius, Constantius III, Joannes, Valentinian III (the most common western solidus of the century, with VICTORIA AVGGG and the emperor treading on a human-headed serpent), Galla Placidia and Honoria, and the later western emperors to Romulus Augustulus. Odoacer and the Ostrogoths kept it: Theodoric and his successors struck gold in the emperor's name with their monograms on silver and bronze, and the city bronze of the 520s-530s shows a turreted personification with FELIX RAVENNA. After 540 Ravenna was the seat of Byzantine Italy (the exarch from the 580s): Byzantine Ravenna solidi are thin and broad with a neat, linear portrait style; bronze reads RAV or RAVENNA. Distinguishing Ravenna, Rome and Constantinople gold of the 6th-7th c. is a specialist skill: compare portrait proportions, lettering and officina markings with the standard catalogues (DOC, MIB, Hahn).

mints.name: Ostia
mints.notes: A short-lived mint created by Maxentius, probably with workers moved from Carthage when Africa revolted under Domitius Alexander (308). Ostia's folles are among the most beautiful of the age: AETERNITAS AVG N with the Dioscuri and their horses, the she-wolf with twins, CONSERV VRB SVAE with Roma in a hexastyle temple, Ostia personified, and the coinage for Divus Romulus (Maxentius' dead son) with the domed shrine. After Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) he struck at Ostia briefly, then moved the staff to Arles in 313. Marks are unambiguous (MOST = Moneta Ostiensis).

mints.name: Carthago (Carthage)
marks: N XLII / N XXI / N XII (Vandal)
mints.notes: Diocletian opened a mint at Carthage c. 296 for the African provinces, with the distinctive types SALVIS AVGG ET CAESS FEL KART (Carthage holding fruit) and FELIX ADVENT AVGG NN for Maximian's African campaign (297/8). It struck for Maxentius after 306, then for the usurper L. Domitius Alexander (308-310), whose folles are rare and much faked, and closed after Maxentius' recovery of Africa (310-311). The Vandals (from 439) struck silver and bronze, at first in the names of Honorius, later with royal names (Gunthamund, Thrasamund, Hilderic, Gelimer) and value marks: silver of 100, 50 and 25 denarii, and bronze of 42, 21 and 12 nummi (N XLII, N XXI, N XII), the latter partly anticipating Anastasius' reform. Justinian's reconquest (533) restored an imperial mint whose output to the 690s is a large and characterful series: small, thick 'globular' gold under Heraclius, folles and half-folles with CAR or KRTG, and 7th-century solidi and silver often carrying indictional dates. Carthage fell to the Arabs in 698.

mints.name: Caesarea Mauretaniae (Cherchell): royal mint of Mauretania
mints.notes: Juba II, raised in Rome and set on the Mauretanian throne by Augustus in 25 BC, struck denarii on the Roman standard with Latin legends for himself and Greek for his wife Cleopatra Selene (daughter of Antony and Cleopatra), with Egyptian motifs (crocodile, Isis crown, sistrum) and his own scholarly interests (elephant, cornucopia). Their son Ptolemy continued, dating coins by regnal year (R A I to R A XX), until Caligula had him killed in 40 and annexed the kingdom. These are among the most attractive client-king denarii; Cleopatra Selene's pieces are scarce and widely faked.

mints.name: Carnuntum: mint of Regalianus
mints.notes: In 260, after the capture of Valerian, the Pannonian commander Regalianus was proclaimed and briefly ruled before being killed. His antoniniani, and those of his wife Sulpicia Dryantilla, were improvised by overstriking old denarii of the Severan age, whose undertypes can often still be read; the flans are small and thick and the engraving crude. Found mainly around Carnuntum, they are attributed to a local emergency mint. All are rare, and modern forgeries exist; an authentic piece should show traces of the host denarius and a crude, provincial style.

mints.name: Siscia (Sisak)
marks: P S T Q V VI (Gallienus-Claudius)
mints.notes: Gallienus opened Siscia c. 262; it became one of the busiest bronze mints of the empire. 3rd-c. radiates carry officina numerals and, after Aurelian's reform, XXI with letters. Its Constantinian and Valentinianic issues are notorious among specialists for an enormous range of field marks (letters, symbols, wreaths, crescents and combinations), which define dozens of small issues of the GLORIA ROMANORVM and SECVRITAS REIPVBLICAE types of 364-378. Siscia struck gold and silver for Licinius and Constantine, Vetranio (350, whose HOC SIGNO VICTOR ERIS bronze with a labarum is struck here and at Thessalonica), Constantius II and the Valentinianic house. Closed c. 387. Identification: Greek officina letters precede SIS (ASIS), whereas Rome and Arles use Latin letters.

mints.name: Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica)
mints.notes: An imperial residence with an intermittent mint. Constantine opened it c. 320 while preparing for the war with Licinius; it struck CAESARVM NOSTRORVM VOT X and the camp-gate PROVIDENTIAE types and fine gold. Constantius II revived it during the war with Magnentius (351, Mursa was nearby). Valentinian I and Valens struck gold and bronze there in the 360s-370s, and a final burst of solidi and bronzes for Theodosius and his sons came in 393-395. In the 5th-6th centuries Sirmium passed through Hunnic, Gepid and Ostrogothic hands, and some pseudo-imperial Gepid issues are attributed to it. Sirmium coins are scarcer than those of Siscia and Thessalonica.

mints.name: Catania (Byzantine Sicily)
mints.notes: A Byzantine bronze mint in Sicily, opened under Maurice (c. 582) and closed under Heraclius. It struck folles (M), half-folles and smaller pieces with CAT/KAT. Catanian folles of Maurice and Phocas are often of large module but irregular manufacture, and many Heraclian coins in Sicily are overstrikes. Its output was replaced by the Sicilian mint whose coins read SCL (probably at Syracuse).

mints.name: Syracusae: the Byzantine Sicilian mint (SCL)
mints.notes: From late in Heraclius' reign a Sicilian mint marked SCL (Sicilia) struck folles, and later 7th-century gold and silver of a distinctive style is attributed to it. It is normally placed at Syracuse, the island's administrative centre (later briefly the residence of Constans II, 663-668). Sicilian Heraclian folles are often overstruck on older coins, sometimes on coins of other mints, and show Heraclius with his son(s) standing. Most of the mint's history falls after 641.
